decks.title: SFM: Introduction
decks.description: Recall cards for CMA Final Paper 14, Chapter 5: Introduction.

fields.definition_md: The first stage of the investment decision process. It values individual securities and compares that value with the price quoted in the market, so that the investor can decide whether to buy, hold or sell.

fields.term: Security and portfolio (as used in security analysis)
fields.definition_md: A security is an instrument of borrowing, lending or contributing funds to a corporate or non-corporate body. A portfolio is a combination of securities with different risk and return characteristics.

fields.prompt_md: Name the two basic approaches to security analysis and say which one this module's first part covers.
fields.answer_md: Fundamental analysis and technical analysis. The first part of the module (5.1) deals with fundamental analysis; technical analysis follows in 5.2.

fields.definition_md: Finds the intrinsic value of a share from the company's profit and dividend prospects, by studying the forces behind the economy, the industry and the company. The decision comes from comparing intrinsic value with market price.

fields.prompt_md: What are the three levels (steps) of fundamental analysis?
fields.answer_md: Economic analysis (the whole economy), industry analysis (the sector the company belongs to) and company analysis (qualitative and quantitative study of the firm itself).

fields.expands_md: Economy, Industry, Company: the order of fundamental analysis in the top-down method.

fields.definition_md: The real worth of a security, distinct from its quoted market price and from book value. It also takes in items such as brand name, trademarks and copyrights, which are hard to measure and may not be visible in the market price.

fields.prompt_md: How does intrinsic value differ from market capitalisation?
fields.answer_md: Market capitalisation is the price, what investors are currently willing to pay for the company. Intrinsic value is the value, what the company is actually worth. Fundamental analysis looks for gaps between the two.

fields.prompt_md: Explain the top-down approach to fundamental analysis.
fields.answer_md: Begin with the economy (GDP, inflation, interest rates, political stability), then narrow to the industry (its nature, demand, government policy), and finish with the individual company (profitability, efficiency, growth prospects).

fields.prompt_md: Explain the bottom-up approach to fundamental analysis.
fields.answer_md: The investor goes directly to the company: its products, competitive position and financial status are studied to estimate earnings potential and hence its market value. The emphasis is on finding companies with good growth prospects and estimating their earnings accurately.

fields.prompt_md: Under the bottom-up approach, what are the two categories of research and how is each described?
fields.answer_md: Growth investing and value investing. Growth stocks carry expectations of above-average earnings growth and trade at high P/E multiples. Value stocks are cheap assets with strong balance sheets.

fields.prompt_md: Which of the two fundamental approaches does the book prefer, and why does bottom-up research often blur growth and value?
fields.answer_md: The book calls the top-down approach the better one. In many cases bottom-up investing makes no clear line between growth and value stocks.

fields.prompt_md: List the assumptions on which technical analysis studies share price movements.
fields.answer_md: There is a basic trend in price movements; the trend repeats itself; and prices have little link with intrinsic value, being driven more by investor psychology and perception.

fields.prompt_md: What is the stated purpose of technical analysis in relation to the company and its industry?
fields.answer_md: To judge the company's relative strength against others in the industry from share price movement, helping the investor decide whether to buy or sell its securities.

fields.prompt_md: Why does economic analysis come first in the top-down approach?
fields.answer_md: Companies and sectors operate inside the overall economy. When the economy is growing sustainably, industry groups and firms benefit and grow faster, so macro conditions help explain share price behaviour.

fields.prompt_md: List the macroeconomic factors commonly analysed in economic analysis.
fields.answer_md: Business cycles, GDP, savings and investment, inflation, interest rates, government budget and expenditure, tax structure, balance of payments, foreign exchange reserves, monsoon and agriculture, infrastructure, demographics and political stability.

fields.definition_md: The recurring pattern of economic expansion and contraction (recession and recovery). The length and depth of the swings are irregular.

The market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a year. It shows the growth rate of the economy and counts only final sales at current value, not the intermediate sales between producer and retailer.

fields.prompt_md: Why is a higher GDP growth rate good for the share market, and what does GDP leave out?
fields.answer_md: Faster growth means more economic activity and better prospects for companies. GDP measures only current-year production, and counts final sale value, so it leaves out intermediate transactions.

fields.prompt_md: How do savings and investment link the economy to the stock market?
fields.answer_md: Growth produces domestic savings, and the stock market is the channel that makes those savings available to industry. The public's savings and investment pattern therefore affects the market.

fields.prompt_md: How does inflation affect capital markets and the valuation of financial assets?
fields.answer_md: Inflation reduces the value of fixed-income securities, pushes nominal interest rates up when expected inflation rises, and adds uncertainty to business and investment decisions. A steady mild inflation is seen as positive and supports market prices.

fields.definition_md: A trend of rising prices caused by demand exceeding supply. Even a small yearly rise cuts the purchasing power of fixed incomes over time.

fields.prompt_md: What is the effect of rising interest rates on borrowing, bonds and share prices?
fields.answer_md: Higher rates cut borrowing and slow the economy. Bond yields move against prices, corporate profitability falls and equity investors apply a higher discount rate, so share prices are hit adversely.

fields.prompt_md: What does the interest rate represent, and give examples of types of interest rates.
fields.answer_md: It is the price of credit: the percentage fee paid or received when money is lent or borrowed. Examples are the bank prime lending rate and the treasury bill rate.

fields.prompt_md: How do budget deficits and surpluses affect the stock market?
fields.answer_md: A deficit (spending above revenue) may lead to high inflation and raise production costs. A surplus may cause deflation. A balanced budget is the most favourable for the stock market.

fields.prompt_md: What counts as government expenditure in this context, and what is excluded?
fields.answer_md: Spending in the budgets of central, state and local governments for infrastructure, research, defence, schools, hospitals and similar goods and services. Relief or compensation payments are excluded because they do not produce goods or services.

fields.prompt_md: What are the main sources of government revenue mentioned in the book?
fields.answer_md: Direct taxes (income tax, corporate tax) and indirect taxes such as GST.

fields.prompt_md: What kind of tax structure helps the market?
fields.answer_md: One that gives incentives for savings and investment.

fields.definition_md: A systematic record of all economic transactions between residents of the reporting country and residents of other countries during a given period. It is grouped into the current account, the capital account and the official international reserve account.

fields.prompt_md: How does the balance of payments determine foreign exchange reserves?
fields.answer_md: A net surplus on both current and capital accounts adds to reserves. When the current account deficit is larger than capital account inflows, the shortfall is met by drawing on reserves. Reserves thus follow the BoP position.

fields.prompt_md: What do foreign exchange reserves consist of?
fields.answer_md: Holdings of foreign currencies (usually hard currencies like the dollar, euro and pound), gold and special drawing rights (SDRs).

fields.prompt_md: Why do monsoon and agriculture matter for Indian share prices?
fields.answer_md: Agriculture is linked directly and indirectly with industry: sugar, textile and food processing use its raw material, and fertiliser and tractor makers supply its inputs. A good monsoon improves harvests and the economy's performance.

fields.prompt_md: Which items does the book list under infrastructure, and what is its importance?
fields.answer_md: Transport, energy, banking and communication. They are essential for the growth of industry and agriculture, and the book says they are still inadequate in India.

fields.prompt_md: What is the use of demographic data in economic analysis?
fields.answer_md: Population by age, occupation, literacy and location helps forecast the demand for consumer goods.

fields.prompt_md: Why is political stability treated as a macro factor?
fields.answer_md: A stable political system is needed for good economic performance; uncertainty and adverse changes in government policy hurt industrial growth.

fields.prompt_md: Name the two techniques used in economic analysis.
fields.answer_md: The economic model building approach (GNP model building or sectoral analysis through the national accounting framework) and gross national product (GNP) analysis.

fields.prompt_md: Describe the steps of the economic model building approach.
fields.answer_md: 1) Hypothesise total economic demand by measuring total income (GNP) in the light of political stability, inflation and other conditions. 2) Forecast the individual components of GNP. 3) Add them up to get the GNP forecast. 4) Compare it with an independent agency's forecast and test it for consistency.

fields.prompt_md: Which components are forecast separately in GNP model building?
fields.answer_md: Consumption expenditure, gross private domestic investment, government purchases of goods and services, and net exports.

fields.name: GNP by the expenditure method (as listed in the model building steps)
fields.variables_md: $C$ = consumption expenditure, $I$ = gross private domestic investment, $G$ = government purchases, $X-M$ = net exports.
fields.when_md: Last step of the economic model building approach: sum the forecast components.

fields.prompt_md: Why is GNP regarded as a forecasting tool in economic analysis?
fields.answer_md: As a measure of national income it reflects the growth rate of economic activity, and it is used to study the whole economy and its components over a period.

fields.prompt_md: In one month 7 of 10 leading indicators rose. What is the diffusion index and how is it computed?
fields.answer_md: Diffusion index = indicators that rose / total indicators observed x 100 = 7/10 x 100 = 70%. A reading above 50% suggests most indicators are pointing up.

fields.definition_md: Study of the specific industry a company belongs to, as opposed to the economy as a whole. It looks at the industry's characteristics, demand, government policy, labour, management and future prospects.

fields.prompt_md: List the factors an industry analysis should take into account.
fields.answer_md: Characteristics of the industry, demand and market, government policy, labour and other industrial problems, management, and future prospects.

fields.prompt_md: Why do the characteristics of an industry matter (seasonality, consumer products, nature of industry)?
fields.answer_md: Seasonal demand can spoil growth prospects. For consumer products the scale of production and width of the market decide selling and advertising cost. The nature of the industry also sets the scale of operation and profitability.

fields.prompt_md: What condition on demand does the book give for an industry to have good profit prospects?
fields.answer_md: Demand for the product should not be controlled by the government.

fields.prompt_md: Which government policy aspects are relevant to industry analysis?
fields.answer_md: The industrial policy resolution and later announcements, covering licences and clearances, installed capacity, pricing, distribution of the product and reservation of products for small industry.

fields.prompt_md: How do labour and marketing problems affect an investor's view of an industry?
fields.answer_md: Labour productivity and capital efficiency determine the industry's progress, so an industry with labour problems should be avoided; marketing problems also call for caution.

fields.prompt_md: What should an investor look at regarding management in industry analysis?
fields.answer_md: For new industries, the project reports and financial institutions' assessments. Management capability shows in tax planning, innovation of technology and modernisation, and good management ensures well-distributed shares with assured liquidity.

fields.prompt_md: Name the techniques used in industry analysis.
fields.answer_md: Regression analysis (with correlation) and input-output analysis.

fields.prompt_md: How is regression analysis used in industry analysis?
fields.answer_md: The investor identifies factors that drive demand for the industry's output (GNP, disposable income, per capita consumption or income, price elasticity of demand) and uses regression and correlation to forecast demand.

fields.prompt_md: What does input-output analysis show and what is it used for?
fields.answer_md: It traces the flow of goods and services through the economy, including the intermediate steps from raw material to final consumption. It is used to detect changing patterns that signal growth or decline of industries.

fields.definition_md: A way of predicting industry sales and profit trends by dividing the industry's development into stages like a human life: birth, adolescence, adulthood, middle age and old age.

fields.prompt_md: Name the five stages of the industry life cycle in order.
fields.answer_md: 1) Pioneering development, 2) rapid accelerating growth, 3) mature growth, 4) stabilisation (market maturity), 5) decline.

fields.prompt_md: To estimate industry sales from the life cycle, what must the investor predict?
fields.answer_md: How long each stage will last: how long growth will accelerate, how long the mature growth phase will run, when growth stabilises and when decline begins.

fields.prompt_md: What does the profit margin typically do across the whole life cycle compared with sales growth?
fields.answer_md: Profit margins need not follow sales growth. They typically peak very early in the cycle and then level off and decline, as competitors are drawn in by early success.

fields.prompt_md: Describe the pioneering development stage.
fields.answer_md: A start-up stage with modest sales growth and very small or negative profits. The market is small and firms bear heavy development costs.

fields.prompt_md: Describe the rapid accelerating growth stage.
fields.answer_md: Markets develop and demand becomes substantial. Few firms face little competition, order backlogs build up and profit margins are very high and rising as firms become efficient. Capacity is built up to meet excess demand.

fields.prompt_md: Describe the mature growth stage.
fields.answer_md: Most demand has been met, so sales still grow faster than the economy but no longer accelerate. High growth and margins attract competitors, supply rises and prices fall, so margins slide back towards normal.

fields.prompt_md: Describe the stabilisation (maturity) stage.
fields.answer_md: Growth moderates. This is probably the longest stage. Products become standard and less innovative, competitors crowd the market and costs are stable. Cost control and operating efficiency drive company margins, and returns on assets and equity settle at or slightly below competitive level.

fields.prompt_md: Describe the decline stage.
fields.answer_md: Sales growth falls because demand shifts or substitutes appear. Margins are squeezed, some firms make low profits or losses, and investors start looking for alternative uses of capital. Product obsolescence is a major reason.

fields.prompt_md: Give the book's example of product obsolescence driving an industry into decline.
fields.answer_md: The steady replacement of desktop computers first by laptops and later by tablets.

fields.prompt_md: Illustrate the 'above normal' growth of the mature growth stage with a number example of your own.
fields.answer_md: If the overall economy grows at 6% a year, an industry in mature growth might see sales growing at 10% to 12%: above normal, but no longer accelerating.

fields.prompt_md: What did Porter say determines the ability of firms to earn above-average returns, and how does he describe competitive strategy?
fields.answer_md: The competitive environment of the industry decides whether firms can sustain above-average returns on invested capital. Competitive strategy is a firm's search for a favourable competitive position within its industry.

fields.prompt_md: List the competitive forces in the book's treatment of Porter's analysis.
fields.answer_md: Threat of new entrants, rivalry between existing competitors, pressure from substitute products and bargaining power of buyers. (Porter's full model also includes bargaining power of suppliers.)

fields.prompt_md: Name Porter's fifth force, which the book's text does not list but its exercise refers to.
fields.answer_md: Bargaining power of suppliers. Powerful suppliers can raise input prices and squeeze industry margins, just as powerful buyers push prices down.

fields.prompt_md: Why does the threat of new entrants matter even before a firm actually enters an industry?
fields.answer_md: The mere possibility of entry puts pressure on prices, because high prices and margins encourage new competitors. Barriers to entry are therefore a key determinant of industry profitability.

fields.prompt_md: List the barriers to entry given in the book.
fields.answer_md: Economies of scale, brand loyalty, government regulation, customer switching costs, absolute cost advantage, ease of distribution, strong capital base and patent protection.

fields.text_md: Barriers to entry include {{c1::economies of scale}}, {{c2::brand loyalty}}, {{c3::switching costs}}, {{c4::capital requirements}} and {{c5::patent protection}}.

fields.prompt_md: In a multiple-choice question on Porter's structural analysis, which of these is not an entry barrier: product differentiation, switching costs, capital requirements, low value addition?
fields.answer_md: Low value addition. Product differentiation, switching costs and capital requirements all make it harder for newcomers to enter.

fields.prompt_md: How does rivalry between existing competitors affect an industry's profits?
fields.answer_md: With many competitors there is generally more price competition and lower profit margins, as each tries to enlarge its market share.

fields.prompt_md: When is rivalry among existing competitors likely to be intense, in Porter's model?
fields.answer_md: When competitors are numerous or equally balanced in strength, and when industry growth is slow so firms must take share from each other. High industry growth eases rivalry.

fields.prompt_md: How do substitute products limit an industry's profitability?
fields.answer_md: They bring competition from firms in related industries and cap the prices that can be charged. Example: wool producers compete with synthetic fibre makers.

fields.prompt_md: When do buyers have strong bargaining power over an industry, and what is the result?
fields.answer_md: When a buyer takes a large share of the industry's output it can demand price concessions. Example: auto makers pressing auto-parts suppliers, which lowers that industry's profitability.

fields.prompt_md: Why must investors keep reviewing the competitive structure of an industry?
fields.answer_md: The competitive structure changes over time, so analysis of competitive forces must be updated to keep the estimate of long-run profit potential current.

fields.prompt_md: How do the economy's expansion and contraction affect industries?
fields.answer_md: Industries generally do better when the economy expands and worse when it contracts, but each industry is different (for example cement is unlike software or textiles in products and processes).

fields.definition_md: Assessment of a firm's competitive position, earnings and profitability, operating efficiency, financial position and its future earnings for shareholders, studying both qualitative and quantitative variables.

fields.prompt_md: What does the economic and industry framework give the investor before company analysis starts?
fields.answer_md: The background against which the shares of a particular company are bought. Company analysis then examines the firm's own quantitative and qualitative fundamentals.

fields.definition_md: Examination of a firm's Strengths, Weaknesses (internal factors) and Opportunities, Threats (external factors).

fields.prompt_md: In SWOT, which elements are internal and which external, and which are positive or negative?
fields.answer_md: Strengths and weaknesses are internal; opportunities and threats are external. Strengths and opportunities are positive; weaknesses and threats are negative.

fields.prompt_md: Give examples of strengths in a SWOT analysis.
fields.answer_md: Technological skill, leading brands, distribution channels, customer loyalty, production quality, scale, strong management, innovative R&D, market leadership or strong financial resources.

fields.prompt_md: Give examples of weaknesses, opportunities and threats in a SWOT analysis.
fields.answer_md: Weaknesses: missing skills, weak brands, poor distribution access, low customer retention, unreliable product, sub-scale operations. Opportunities: changing customer tastes, technological advances, favourable policy, lower personal taxes, new distribution channels. Threats: change in customer base, closing markets, tax increases, adverse policy changes.

fields.prompt_md: How should a company treat its strengths to keep them?
fields.answer_md: Keep developing, maintaining and defending them through prudent capital investment policies.

fields.prompt_md: List the factors considered in company analysis.
fields.answer_md: Net worth and book value; sources and utilisation of funds; time series, common size and ratio analysis; size and ranking; growth record; quality of management; location and labour-management relations; pattern of stock holding; marketability of shares.

fields.text_md: Company analysis factors include {{c1::net worth and book value}}, {{c2::growth record}}, {{c3::quality of management}}, {{c4::pattern of shareholding}} and {{c5::marketability of shares}}.

fields.name: Net worth of the business (for book value)
fields.variables_md: Net worth is the amount available to equity shareholders.
fields.when_md: First step in company analysis; divide by shares outstanding to get book value per share.

fields.prompt_md: Compute the net worth and book value per share: equity capital 10,00,000, free reserves 4,00,000, accumulated losses 1,00,000, and 1,00,000 shares outstanding.
Why may book value fail to indicate a share's intrinsic worth?
fields.answer_md: First, market price reflects future earning potential, which can be unrelated to asset value (as in the service sector). Second, book value uses historical cost, which can badly understate replacement or resale value of assets.

fields.prompt_md: What is the purpose of analysing sources and utilisation of funds, and what danger does it expose?
fields.answer_md: Fund flow and cash flow analysis shows whether short-term funds have financed long-term investments. That raises liquidity risk, because long-gestation investments may not yield surplus in time to repay short-term liabilities, which increases credit and default risk.

fields.prompt_md: Which techniques are used for comparative analysis of financial statements?
fields.answer_md: Common-size statements, financial ratio analysis and time series analysis. They support inter-firm and intra-firm comparison.

fields.prompt_md: Why does the size and ranking of a company matter to an investment manager?
fields.answer_md: A rough idea of the firm's size and rank in the economy and in its industry helps assess its risk. It also shows its position in technical know-how, R&D and price leadership.

fields.prompt_md: What should be examined under growth record?
fields.answer_md: Growth over the past few years in sales, net income, net capital employed and earnings per share.

fields.prompt_md: Why is quality of management important, and how is it reflected in the share price?
fields.answer_md: It is an intangible factor with a strong bearing on share value. Management quality shows up in the confidence investors have in the company, which is reflected in its share price.

fields.prompt_md: Why do location and labour-management relations matter in company analysis?
fields.answer_md: Location decides economic viability: nearness to markets and availability of power, skilled labour and raw materials. Good labour relations affect operating efficiency.

fields.prompt_md: Why analyse the pattern of existing stockholding?
fields.answer_md: To know the stake of the various parties in the company.

fields.prompt_md: Why is a share's listing not enough to guarantee marketability, and what is market depth?
fields.answer_md: Many listed shares stay inactive for long periods with no trades. Market depth is the dispersal of shareholding, especially the extent of public holding. Speculative interest, the exchange of trading and trading volume also matter.

fields.prompt_md: Name the techniques used in company analysis.
fields.answer_md: Correlation and regression analysis, time series and trend analysis, and decision tree analysis.

fields.prompt_md: When is simple regression used and when is multiple regression used in company analysis?
fields.answer_md: Simple regression when the relationship involves two variables; multiple regression when there are more than two. They relate economy, industry and company variables, quantified using correlation coefficients and standard deviations.

fields.prompt_md: How is time series and trend analysis carried out?
fields.answer_md: A trend line (characteristic line) is fitted by the method of least squares to a given time series, and the trend is extrapolated.

fields.prompt_md: What is decision tree analysis in company analysis?
fields.answer_md: It uses probability: probabilities are assigned to states of nature and the expected value of each course of action is computed.

fields.prompt_md: Why are tools applied to financial statement data in fundamental analysis?
fields.answer_md: Raw statement figures carry some information, but applying tools (ratios and models) to them reveals much more about a stock's value.

fields.name: Earnings per share (EPS)
fields.expression_md: $\text{EPS} = \dfrac{\text{Total earnings available to equity shareholders}}{\text{Number of equity shares outstanding}}$
fields.variables_md: Earnings available to equity shareholders = profit after tax less preference dividend.
fields.when_md: Base for the P/E ratio, the earnings approach to share valuation and the dividend payout ratio.

fields.name: Price-earnings (P/E) ratio
fields.variables_md: Market price per share and EPS for the same share.
fields.when_md: Shows how much the market pays for each rupee of earnings. A high P/E reflects growth expectations.

fields.prompt_md: Equity earnings of Rs 6,00,000 on 1,50,000 shares and a market price of Rs 56. Find EPS and P/E.
What does a high P/E ratio signal and what is the reciprocal of P/E?
fields.answer_md: A high P/E means investors are paying a lot per rupee of earnings, usually because they expect growth. The reciprocal (EPS / price) is the earnings yield, which equals the normal rate of return in the EPS valuation method.

fields.name: PEG ratio
fields.variables_md: Growth is entered as a whole number (12 for 12%).
fields.when_md: Adjusts P/E for growth. A lower PEG indicates a stock that is more undervalued.

fields.prompt_md: A share has P/E of 18 and expected annual EPS growth of 12%. Compute PEG and say how to read it.
fields.answer_md: PEG = 18 / 12 = 1.5. Compare it with other stocks: the lower the PEG, the cheaper the stock relative to its growth.

fields.prompt_md: Why do many analysts prefer PEG to the P/E ratio?
fields.answer_md: PEG also accounts for earnings growth, so it gives a better picture of potential value than P/E alone. As with P/E, a lower PEG means the stock is more undervalued.

fields.name: Price to sales ratio (P/S)
fields.variables_md: Revenue per share = total revenue / shares outstanding.
fields.when_md: Used when earnings are negative or unreliable.

fields.prompt_md: Share price Rs 90 and revenue per share Rs 45. Find P/S.

fields.name: Price to book ratio (P/B)
fields.variables_md: Book value per share = (shareholders' equity - preference equity) / shares outstanding.
fields.when_md: Compares what the market pays with the accounting worth of each share.

fields.prompt_md: Share price Rs 168, book value per share Rs 120. Find P/B.

fields.name: Dividend yield
fields.expression_md: $\text{Dividend yield} = \dfrac{\text{Annual dividend per share}}{\text{Market price per share}}$
fields.variables_md: Expressed as a percentage return from dividends only.
fields.when_md: Used by investors who want to maximise dividend income.

fields.prompt_md: Dividend per share Rs 6 and market price Rs 120. Find the dividend yield. Which kind of company usually pays a higher yield?
fields.answer_md: Yield = 6 / 120 = 5%. Older, well-established companies usually pay a higher percentage and have a more consistent dividend history than younger ones.

fields.name: Dividend payout ratio
fields.variables_md: Retention ratio = $1 - $ payout ratio.
fields.when_md: Shows what share of earnings is paid out; mature companies tend to have a higher payout.

fields.prompt_md: DPS is Rs 3 and EPS is Rs 12. Find the payout and the retention ratio, and say what the payout tells you.
fields.answer_md: Payout = 3 / 12 = 25%; retention = 75%. The payout ratio shows how well earnings support the dividend.

fields.name: Book value per share
fields.variables_md: Equity less preference capital is what belongs to ordinary shareholders.
fields.when_md: Measures the safety cushion per share after all debts and preference claims are met.

fields.prompt_md: Shareholders' equity is Rs 12,00,000, of which preference equity is Rs 2,00,000, with 50,000 shares outstanding. Find BVPS.

fields.name: DuPont model of ROE
fields.variables_md: Net margin $\times$ asset turnover $\times$ equity multiplier (leverage).
fields.when_md: Breaks ROE into drivers so you can see which area of the business changed return on equity.

fields.prompt_md: Net margin is 8%, asset turnover 1.5 times and the equity multiplier 2. Find ROE using DuPont.
Under the DuPont model, what makes ROE rise, all else equal?
fields.answer_md: A higher net margin, more revenue generated from the firm's assets (higher asset turnover), and more leverage.

fields.prompt_md: Why does greater leverage raise ROE in the DuPont model?
fields.answer_md: If revenue-generating assets are bought with debt rather than equity, the extra net income from more assets is earned on an unchanged amount of equity, so the return on equity increases.

fields.name: ROE from ROA and leverage
fields.variables_md: ROA = return on assets; leverage factor = total assets / equity.
fields.when_md: Short route used in practical MCQs.

fields.prompt_md: ROA is 12% and the leverage factor is 1.5. Find ROE. Separately, ROE is 20% and BVPS is Rs 30: find EPS.
fields.answer_md: ROE = 12% x 1.5 = 18%. Since ROE = EPS / BVPS, EPS = 20% x 30 = Rs 6.

fields.name: Sustainable growth rate
fields.variables_md: Retention ratio = share of net income reinvested; ROE = return on equity.
fields.when_md: Fastest growth a firm can expect from reinvested earnings alone. Also used for the growth rate in dividend growth models.

fields.prompt_md: A company has ROE of 16% and retains 60% of earnings. Find its sustainable growth rate. Another has ROE 20% and payout 40%.
fields.answer_md: First: g = 0.60 x 16% = 9.6%. Second: retention = 60%, so g = 0.60 x 20% = 12%.

fields.prompt_md: Why is the sustainable growth rate capped by ROE?
fields.answer_md: Growth comes from reinvesting net income. If the whole income were retained (retention 100%), growth would equal ROE, which is the fastest it can be.

fields.name: ROE for common shareholders (alternative definition)
fields.variables_md: Preference dividends are removed because they are not available to common shareholders.
fields.when_md: When the question asks for the return earned on the ordinary shareholders' stake.

fields.prompt_md: Net income is Rs 5,00,000, preference dividend Rs 50,000, average equity Rs 30,00,000. Find ROE for common shareholders.
Group the 'other relevant ratios' in the book by category.
fields.answer_md: Liquidity (current, quick, cash); leverage (debt-equity, debt-asset, interest coverage); turnover or management efficiency (inventory, debtors, fixed assets, total assets); profitability (operating margin, net margin, ROA, ROCE, ROE).

fields.name: Current ratio and quick ratio
fields.expression_md: $\text{Current ratio} = \dfrac{\text{Current assets}}{\text{Current liabilities}} \qquad \text{Quick ratio} = \dfrac{\text{Quick assets}}{\text{Current liabilities}}$
fields.variables_md: Quick assets = current assets less inventories (and prepaid items).
fields.when_md: Liquidity ratios: the ability to pay current liabilities. The quick ratio is also called the acid test ratio.

fields.prompt_md: Current assets Rs 5,00,000, inventory Rs 1,50,000, current liabilities Rs 2,50,000. Find the current and quick ratios.

fields.name: Cash ratio
fields.variables_md: Current investments mean marketable securities held for short term.
fields.when_md: The strictest liquidity test.

fields.prompt_md: What does liquidity measure for a company?
fields.answer_md: The ability to pay its current (short-term) liabilities as they fall due.

fields.name: Debt-equity and debt-asset ratios
fields.expression_md: $\text{D/E} = \dfrac{\text{Total outside liabilities}}{\text{Shareholders' funds}} \qquad \text{Debt-asset} = \dfrac{\text{Total outside liabilities}}{\text{Total assets}}$
fields.variables_md: Outside liabilities = all amounts owed to non-owners.
fields.when_md: Leverage ratios, showing how much of the business is financed by outsiders.

fields.name: Interest coverage ratio
fields.variables_md: PBIT = profit before interest and tax.
fields.when_md: Shows how many times operating profit covers interest. The book's table prints total assets in the denominator, which is a misprint.

fields.prompt_md: PBIT is Rs 6,00,000 and interest is Rs 1,50,000. Find the interest coverage. Outside liabilities Rs 8,00,000 and shareholders' funds Rs 4,00,000: find D/E.

fields.name: Inventory turnover ratio
fields.variables_md: Average inventory = (opening + closing) / 2.
fields.when_md: Efficiency of stock management. The book's table puts 'returns from operations' in the numerator; the usual form uses cost of goods sold.

fields.name: Debtors' turnover ratio
fields.variables_md: Credit sales exclude cash sales.
fields.when_md: Speed of collection: higher is better. 360 (or 365) divided by it gives the average collection period in days.

fields.prompt_md: Net credit sales Rs 12,00,000 and average debtors Rs 2,00,000. Find debtors' turnover and the collection period (360-day year).
fields.answer_md: Turnover = 12,00,000 / 2,00,000 = 6 times; collection period = 360 / 6 = 60 days.

fields.name: Fixed assets and total assets turnover
fields.expression_md: $\text{FA turnover} = \dfrac{\text{Revenue from operations}}{\text{Average net fixed assets}} \qquad \text{TA turnover} = \dfrac{\text{Total revenues}}{\text{Average total assets}}$
fields.variables_md: Both use averages of opening and closing balances.
fields.when_md: Measure how effectively assets generate sales.

fields.name: Operating and net profit margin
fields.variables_md: PBIT = profit before interest and tax.
fields.when_md: Profitability ratios. Net margin is the first DuPont component.

fields.name: Return on assets (ROA)
fields.variables_md: Average of opening and closing total assets.
fields.when_md: Return generated on all assets, before regard to how they are financed.

fields.name: Return on capital employed (ROCE)
fields.variables_md: $T$ = tax rate. Many texts use pre-tax PBIT; check which version the question asks for.
fields.when_md: The book's table shows average total assets in the denominator; capital employed is the usual base.

fields.name: Return on equity (ROE) or return on net worth
fields.variables_md: Equity = shareholders' funds.
fields.when_md: Return earned for owners; the product of the three DuPont components.

fields.prompt_md: Which ratios belong to the turnover or management efficiency group?
fields.answer_md: Inventory turnover, debtors' turnover, fixed assets turnover and total assets turnover.

fields.prompt_md: Name the three methods of share valuation listed in the book.
fields.answer_md: Book value method (balance sheet or net asset value), market value method (yield value, for a going concern) and fair value method.

fields.prompt_md: How does the book define fair value of a share, and what is wrong with that line in the book?
fields.answer_md: Fair value is taken as the average of book value and market value. The book's line prints it as the average of book value and fair value, which is a slip.

fields.name: Fair value of a share (average method)
fields.variables_md: Market value is the yield (going-concern) value from the dividend or earnings method.
fields.when_md: When a question asks for the fair value of a share.

fields.prompt_md: Book value per share is Rs 60 and market value (yield value) is Rs 80. Find fair value.
fields.answer_md: Fair value = (60 + 80) / 2 = Rs 70.

fields.definition_md: Assumes the company is wound up (without liquidation expenses). Value per equity share is what the holder of one share would receive: current value of all assets, including goodwill and non-trade assets, less outside liabilities and the preference shareholders' claim, divided by equity shares.

fields.prompt_md: Which value do accountants call intrinsic value in the book's valuation section?
fields.answer_md: The book value, balance sheet value or net asset value of a share.

fields.name: Net asset value per equity share
fields.expression_md: $\text{NAV per share} = \dfrac{\text{Revalued assets} - \text{Outside liabilities} - \text{Preference claim}}{\text{Number of equity shares}}$
fields.variables_md: Assets include goodwill and non-trade assets at current values; preference claim at the amount payable to them.
fields.when_md: Liquidation basis, ignoring winding-up expenses unless the question states them.

fields.prompt_md: Assets revalue to Rs 20,00,000, outside liabilities are Rs 6,00,000, preference capital Rs 2,00,000, and there are 50,000 equity shares. Find value per equity share.
Outline the steps when preference holders also share in surplus assets on liquidation and equity shares are partly paid.
fields.answer_md: 1) Revalue assets and add the appreciation. 2) Deduct total paid-up capital (preference and equity) to get surplus assets. 3) Give preference holders their stated percentage of the surplus; the rest goes to equity. 4) Divide each by its number of shares. 5) Add back paid-up value per share: preference = paid-up + its surplus share; each equity share = amount paid + equity surplus per share.

fields.prompt_md: Surplus after returning all paid-up capital is Rs 4,00,000; preference holders (2,000 shares) get 10% of surplus; 20,000 equity shares exist. Find surplus per share.
fields.answer_md: Preference surplus = 40,000 so Rs 20 per preference share. Equity surplus = 3,60,000, so Rs 18 per equity share. Each share's value is its paid-up amount plus this.

fields.definition_md: Treats the business as a going concern and values a share from the returns it is expected to give, using either dividends or EPS capitalised at the normal rate of return on equity (Ke).

fields.prompt_md: Which approaches exist under the market value method?
fields.answer_md: One based on dividends (constant dividend, also called dividend yield method, and growing dividend, called dividend growth method) and one based on EPS (also called the P/E method).

fields.name: Market price: constant dividend
fields.variables_md: $D$ = expected annual dividend per share, $K_e$ = normal rate of return on equity.
fields.when_md: Dividend is expected to stay the same forever.

fields.name: Market price: dividend growing at a constant rate
fields.variables_md: $D_1 = D_0(1+g)$ = next year's dividend, $g$ = constant growth rate, $K_e > g$.
fields.when_md: Dividends grow at a steady rate; also called the dividend growth method.

fields.name: Market price: EPS method
fields.variables_md: P/E is the reciprocal of $K_e$.
fields.when_md: Used when dividend data is missing or the question gives a P/E ratio.

fields.prompt_md: Rs 6 constant dividend, Ke 12%. Then D0 = Rs 5, growth 6%, Ke 14%. Then EPS Rs 8, Ke 16%. Find each market price.
fields.answer_md: Constant dividend: 6 / 0.12 = Rs 50. Growth: D1 = 5 x 1.06 = 5.30, price = 5.30 / (0.14 - 0.06) = Rs 66.25. EPS method: 8 / 0.16 = Rs 50 (equal to EPS x P/E of 6.25).

fields.prompt_md: Why should valuation use next year's dividend or EPS rather than last year's?
fields.answer_md: The market always discounts the future, so a share's value depends on future EPS and dividends, not past ones.

fields.prompt_md: If a question does not name a method, in what order should the market value approaches be preferred?
fields.answer_md: First the growth-based (dividend growth) method, then the EPS-based method, then the constant dividend method.

fields.prompt_md: What is Ke in the yield value formulas, and how is it linked to P/E?
fields.answer_md: It is the return investors normally expect on equity shares of that risk. P/E is its reciprocal, so a share valued on EPS with a given normal rate is the same as EPS x P/E.

fields.prompt_md: Outline the method to value a business from a trial balance and forecasts using the P/E approach.
fields.answer_md: 1) Work out last year's cost of goods sold (opening stock + purchases - closing stock) and its percentage of sales. 2) Forecast next year's sales and cost items with the stated changes. 3) Prepare the forecast profit and loss account and find net profit (ignore tax if told). 4) Divide by number of equity shares to get EPS. 5) Multiply by the given P/E ratio to get market price.

fields.prompt_md: Forecast net profit is Rs 12,00,000 on 1,00,000 equity shares and the industry P/E is 9. What is the share's value?
In forecast-based valuation, how do you number the equity shares and what is the EPS?
fields.answer_md: Equity shares = equity share capital / face value per share. EPS = forecast net profit / that number of shares.

fields.prompt_md: How is depreciation adjusted in such forecasts when assets are added during the year?
fields.answer_md: Charge the stated percentage on opening cost for the full year and, on the new asset, only for the part of the year it is used. Always check the time basis the question gives.

fields.definition_md: Forecasting future price movements from an examination of past price movements, using charts of price over time. It does not give absolute predictions, only what is 'likely' to happen, much as weather forecasting does.

fields.prompt_md: To which instruments can technical analysis be applied, and what is meant by 'price'?
fields.answer_md: Stocks, indices, commodities, futures or any tradable instrument whose price is set by supply and demand. Price means any mix of open, high, low or close for a chosen time frame; some analysts also use volume or open interest.

fields.prompt_md: What time frames can technical analysis use?
fields.answer_md: Intraday (1, 5, 10, 15, 30 minutes or hourly), daily, weekly or monthly data, covering a few hours up to many years.

fields.prompt_md: State the three basic premises of technical analysis.
fields.answer_md: Price discounts everything; price movements are not totally random (prices trend); and 'what' (the price) matters more than 'why'.

fields.prompt_md: Explain 'price discounts everything'.
fields.answer_md: The current price already reflects all information from all participants (traders, fund managers, analysts and so on), so it represents fair value. The analyst reads the price to form a view of the future.

fields.prompt_md: Explain the premise that price movements are not totally random.
fields.answer_md: Technicians accept that prices usually trend, though not always. If prices were always random, technical analysis could not make money. A technician aims to spot a trend, trade along it and profit as it unfolds, in both short and long time frames.

fields.prompt_md: Explain why technicians say 'what' is more important than 'why'.
fields.answer_md: They care only about the current price and the history of price movement. Price is the result of the battle between supply and demand; the reasons behind it are too broad and often suspect. A rise simply means more buyers than sellers.

fields.prompt_md: What famous remark about technical analysts does the book quote?
fields.answer_md: Tony Plummer, paraphrasing Oscar Wilde: such an analyst knows what everything costs yet what nothing is worth.

fields.prompt_md: From which four points of view is technical analysis done?
fields.answer_md: Prices, time, volume and width.

fields.expands_md: Price, Time, Volume, Width: the four viewpoints of technical analysis.

fields.prompt_md: Explain price and time in technical analysis.
fields.answer_md: Price: any change in security prices reflects shifts in investor attitude and in demand and supply. Time: the degree of price movement is a function of time; the longer a trend takes to reverse, the greater the price change that follows.

fields.prompt_md: Explain volume and width in technical analysis.
fields.answer_md: Volume: the intensity of a price change is shown by the volume of trading with it; a rise on small volume is not strong. Width: whether a trend spreads across most sectors and industries or only a few securities, showing how broad the market move is.

fields.prompt_md: Differentiate technical analysis from fundamental analysis on time horizon and data used.
fields.answer_md: Technical analysis predicts short-term price moves from internal market data, mainly price and volume. Fundamental analysis establishes long-term value from economy, industry and company factors.

fields.prompt_md: Differentiate technical analysis from fundamental analysis on who uses each and how complex each is.
fields.answer_md: Speculators seeking quick gains mostly use technical analysis; long-term investors use fundamental analysis. Fundamental analysis handles huge data and is complex and time consuming; technical analysis is simple and quick.

fields.prompt_md: What criticisms do technical analysts make of fundamental analysis?
fields.answer_md: It rests on financial statements, which suffer from subjectivity and inadequate disclosure. Also, even if an underpriced security is found, the market may take time to bid its price up, so technicians claim their charts are quicker and superior.

fields.prompt_md: Are technical and fundamental analysis substitutes or complements in practice?
fields.answer_md: Complements. They give opposite approaches to valuation, but in practice a judicious combination of both is used to get better results.

fields.definition_md: The oldest and best-known theory of technical analysis, developed from 1900 by Charles H Dow, editor of the Wall Street Journal. It studies the major market movements to establish trends; a trend is assumed to continue until a reversal occurs.

fields.prompt_md: Who followed up on Dow's work and how?
fields.answer_md: William Hamilton used the theory to predict market movements (Dow built it to describe past moves). Robert Rhea later gave a formal account and tried to measure the size and duration of trends.

fields.prompt_md: What does the Dow Theory describe and what does it not attempt?
fields.answer_md: It describes the direction of market trends. In its original form it does not forecast future movements or estimate their size or duration.

fields.prompt_md: Name the three types of trend (movement) in the Dow Theory with their analogies.
fields.answer_md: Primary (major) trends are like tides in the ocean, intermediate trends are like waves, and short-run movements are like ripples.

fields.text_md: Dow Theory: major trend = {{c1::tide}}, intermediate trend = {{c2::wave}}, short-run movement = {{c3::ripple}}.

fields.prompt_md: Which trend do Dow Theory followers try to detect, and why can intermediate moves go the other way?
fields.answer_md: The primary trend (tide). Intermediate waves may occasionally move against it, since a major advance does not rise straight but includes small declines when investors take profits.

fields.prompt_md: Describe the typical bullish pattern in the Dow Theory.
fields.answer_md: Each recovery makes a new peak above the previous peak, with heavy trading volume. Each profit-taking dip leaves a trough above the previous trough on relatively light volume.

fields.prompt_md: What does it mean if the bullish price and volume pattern stops holding?
fields.answer_md: The major trend may be entering consolidation (a flat trend) or a major reversal.

fields.prompt_md: Define a bull market and a bear market using peaks and bottoms.
fields.answer_md: Bull market: prices rise, with each peak and each bottom higher than the one before. Bear market: a declining market, with lower peaks and lower bottoms.

fields.prompt_md: What are charts useful for in technical analysis?
fields.answer_md: Spotting current trends for buying and selling, projecting probable future market action, showing historical movements and indicating key support and resistance areas.

fields.prompt_md: Why does the book warn that chart reading needs skill?
fields.answer_md: Charts do not lie, but their interpretation differs between analysts according to skill and experience. In James Dines' words, they are like fire or electricity: brilliant when controlled, dangerous to a novice.

fields.prompt_md: Differentiate reversal patterns from continuation patterns.
fields.answer_md: Reversal patterns signal the end of the trend that existed before the pattern formed (an uptrend likely over). Continuation patterns signal that the trend will continue after the pattern completes, with the breakout in the trend's direction.

fields.prompt_md: How do trend lines help with chart patterns?
fields.answer_md: They are drawn along high and low points to highlight a pattern, and a break out of them signals completion. The size of the pattern and where it sits in the trend hint at how big the next move will be.

fields.prompt_md: How is a line chart drawn and how does it relate to a bar chart?
fields.answer_md: Closing prices are plotted daily and joined, with price on the Y-axis and time on the X-axis. It is a simplification of the bar chart, easy to draw and good for spotting patterns.

fields.prompt_md: How is a bar chart built?
fields.answer_md: For each period a dot marks the highest price and another the lowest, and a line joins them. A horizontal tick marks the closing price. It is the simplest and most widely used chart.

fields.prompt_md: Describe the V formation and the inverted V.
fields.answer_md: V: a long sharp fall followed by a quick reversal, common in popular stocks where sentiment swings fast between hope and fear. Inverted V: a rise followed by a decline. Extended V: the bottom or top forms slowly over a broader area.

fields.prompt_md: How should an investor use top and bottom formations, and what do they signal?
fields.answer_md: They form at the start or end of trends: reversals from tops give sell signals and from bottoms give buy signals. Buy after the upward trend starts and exit before the top is reached.

fields.prompt_md: What are double top and double bottom patterns?
fields.answer_md: A double top shows price failing twice at about the same high, a reversal from an uptrend (sell). A double bottom shows two similar lows, a reversal from a downtrend (buy).

fields.prompt_md: How is the classic head and shoulders top formed, and what happens when price falls through its neckline?
fields.answer_md: Three rallies form a left shoulder, a head and a right shoulder, and a neckline joins the lows between them. When price cuts the neckline from above, it signals a bear market. It is easy to identify and regarded as reliable.

fields.prompt_md: What does a break above the neckline of an inverted head and shoulders (a bottom pattern) indicate?
fields.answer_md: The mirror image: price falls and rises forming an inverted head with shoulders; the neckline joins the tips. When price pierces the neckline from below it marks the end of a bear market and the start of a bull market. Confirm with volume and market trend.

fields.prompt_md: Why does the left shoulder form in the head and shoulders pattern?
fields.answer_md: After a rise, those who bought during the upward trend start selling at the top, causing a dip. Near the bottom, those who missed the first rally buy at lower prices, pushing price up again. The alternating demand and supply create new highs and lows.

fields.prompt_md: Describe the rounding bottom pattern and the conditions for it to confirm a reversal.
fields.answer_md: A bullish, elongated U-shape (also called rounding turn, bowl or saucer) showing a possible reversal of a downtrend. The bottom low must be a new low and not too sharp; the fall and rise take about equal time; the breakout must be above the start of the decline; volume is high at the start of the decline, low at the end and rises during the advance.

fields.prompt_md: What are point and figure (P&F) charts and what do they show?
fields.answer_md: Charts used to predict the extent and direction of price moves of a stock or index. They are one-dimensional with no indication of time or volume, showing price changes relative to earlier prices. They are drawn on ruled paper.

fields.prompt_md: Describe a flag pattern.
fields.answer_md: A parallelogram-like pattern appearing before a rise or fall, showing market correction of an over-bought or over-sold situation. It forms quickly, with each rally and setback lasting three to four days, or about three weeks if wider.

fields.prompt_md: How do bullish (up) and bearish (down) flags differ?
fields.answer_md: Bullish flag: both trend lines slope downwards and the breakout comes through the upper line. Bearish flag: both trend lines slope upwards and the breakout comes through the lower line.

fields.prompt_md: Describe bullish and bearish pennants.
fields.answer_md: A pennant looks like a symmetrical triangle. In the bullish pennant the upper trend line connects lower tops and the lower line connects rising bottoms; the bullish move occurs when price breaks above the upper line. In the bearish pennant the upper line is falling, the lower one rising, and the breakout is downward.

fields.prompt_md: What four elements are needed to draw a candlestick chart?
fields.answer_md: Open, high, low and closing prices for the period.

fields.prompt_md: How is a candlestick body coloured, and what does each colour imply?
fields.answer_md: White body: close is above the open, a bullish trend. Black body: close is below the open, a bearish trend.

fields.prompt_md: Who is credited with the early use of candlestick charts?
fields.answer_md: Munehisa Homma, a rice merchant of Sakata in Japan in the 1700s, who used them to forecast rice prices. The book calls them the oldest price prediction charts.

fields.prompt_md: State the Elliott Wave Theory in brief.
fields.answer_md: Ralph Nelson Elliott (late 1920s) said that although markets look chaotic, trading happens in repetitive cycles. A cycle is five waves in the main trend plus three corrective waves (a 5-3 pattern). The 5-3 pattern stays constant while the time span of each wave can vary.

fields.prompt_md: Which Elliott waves are impulsive and which corrective?
fields.answer_md: Waves 1, 3 and 5 move in the direction of the main trend and are impulsive. Waves 2, 4 and B are corrective. The book also calls A and C impulsive because they run with the move of the correction.

fields.text_md: An Elliott cycle has {{c1::five}} impulsive waves numbered 1 to 5 and {{c2::three}} corrective waves labelled A to C.

fields.prompt_md: In which markets does the Elliott pattern apply?
fields.answer_md: In a bull market the five-wave advance is followed by a three-wave decline; for a bear market the same pattern runs downward.

fields.prompt_md: How is Elliott Wave Theory related to the Dow Theory?
fields.answer_md: Both say prices move in waves, but Elliott adds a fixed repeating structure of five waves with the trend and three against it.

fields.definition_md: An oscillator developed by Wells Wilder to identify the inherent technical strength or weakness of a scrip or market. It foretells reactionary or sustained rises and falls in price.

fields.name: Relative Strength Index
fields.expression_md: $\text{RSI} = 100 - \dfrac{100}{1 + RS}, \quad RS = \dfrac{\text{Average gain per day}}{\text{Average loss per day}}$
fields.variables_md: Average gain = total of up-day gains / number of days; average loss = total of down-day losses / number of days, over the chosen period (for example 14 days).
fields.when_md: Used to judge overbought and oversold conditions; appears as numerical MCQs in the exam.

fields.prompt_md: Over a period the average gain per day is Rs 2 and the average loss per day is Rs 0.50. Find RS and RSI.
Method: how do you compute RSI from a table of daily closing prices?
fields.answer_md: 1) Find each day's change from the previous close. 2) Add up all gains (up days) and all losses (down days, as positive numbers). 3) Divide each total by the number of days in the period to get average gain and average loss. 4) RS = average gain / average loss. 5) RSI = 100 - 100/(1+RS).

fields.prompt_md: Over 14 days the up-day gains total Rs 21 and the down-day losses total Rs 14. Find RSI.
Which period lengths is RSI calculated for and what is the effect of a longer period?
fields.answer_md: 5, 7, 9 and 14 days are used, depending on the analyst and trading time frame. A longer period reduces the chance of getting a wrong signal.

fields.prompt_md: What RSI levels are commonly read as overbought and oversold?
fields.answer_md: Above 70 is usually read as overbought (a possible fall) and below 30 as oversold (a possible rise). These levels are market convention, not stated in this book's text.

fields.definition_md: A momentum indicator, developed by George C Lane in the late 1950s, showing where the closing price sits within the high-low range of a chosen period. Rising prices tend to close near the high, falling prices near the low.

fields.name: Stochastic %K (fast stochastic)
fields.variables_md: $C$ = latest closing price, $L_n$ = lowest price in the last $n$ periods, $H_n$ = highest price in the last $n$ periods.
fields.when_md: Gives a value between 0 and 100 showing the close's position in the range. The book omits the formula in its text, so this is the standard one.

fields.prompt_md: Closing price Rs 130, 20-day low Rs 100, 20-day high Rs 150. Find stochastic %K.
Closing price Rs 95, 50-day low Rs 80, 50-day high Rs 110. Find %K and say where the close sits.
What are the %K and %D lines of the stochastic indicator?
fields.answer_md: Both oscillate between 0 and 100. %K is the faster line, %D lags behind it (%D is a moving average of %K). The %D line is used to identify overbought and oversold zones.

fields.prompt_md: Distinguish the fast and slow stochastic.
fields.answer_md: Fast stochastic uses the raw %K and is considered too jumpy for in-day trading, so the slow stochastic smooths it: the fast %D becomes the slow %K, and the slow %D is a three-day simple moving average of slow %K.

fields.prompt_md: Raw %K readings on three days are 40, 55 and 70. Find the three-day SMA used for %D.
State the overbought and oversold zones of the stochastic oscillator, and the best buy and sell levels.
fields.answer_md: Overbought above 70 and oversold below 30 on the %D line. The best buy signals come below 15 and the best sell signals above 85.

fields.text_md: Stochastic: overbought above {{c1::70}}, oversold below {{c2::30}}; best buy signals below {{c3::15}}, best sell signals above {{c4::85}}.

fields.prompt_md: How do %K and %D crossovers generate stochastic buy and sell signals?
fields.answer_md: Sell: %D is in the overbought zone and %K crosses it from above. Buy: in the oversold zone %K moves above %D. Signals in the direction of the major trend of the scrip are powerful.

fields.prompt_md: Why does %K in the extreme zones matter for %D?
fields.answer_md: %K in the overbought or oversold zone gives an early hint that the slower %D line may follow it there.

fields.definition_md: The average of a stock's price over a fixed number of recent periods (for example 50 days), recalculated as each new period arrives. It smooths out day-to-day swings and shows the underlying trend. The book asks about it only in the exercise.

fields.prompt_md: What buy signals does moving average analysis give, as asked in a past exam MCQ?
fields.answer_md: Chandra's rules treat these as buy signals: price rising through a flattening or rising MA line; price falling below an MA line that is rising (a dip in an uptrend); and a price below a falling MA that turns up before reaching the line. Mirror images are the sell signals.

fields.prompt_md: In a two-MA setup (50-day and 200-day), what does a bearish pattern look like?
fields.answer_md: The shorter 50-day line crosses below the 200-day line (a death cross) with price falling below both, suggesting a downtrend. The opposite crossover, the golden cross, is bullish. The book only sets this as an essay question.

fields.definition_md: A price level at which buying demand is strong enough to halt a fall in price. Technicians watch for price to hold or break it.
A price level at which selling pressure is strong enough to halt a rise in price. A decisive break above it is read as bullish.

fields.prompt_md: What does 'violation of a trend line' mean?
fields.answer_md: The price penetrates (cuts through) the trend line, which may signal a change of direction.

fields.prompt_md: Where does the stock price move relative to support and resistance in the book's MCQ?
fields.answer_md: Between changing support and resistance levels (the levels shift as the trend moves).

fields.prompt_md: List the main disadvantage points a student could use to criticise fundamental analysis in favour of technical analysis.
fields.answer_md: It handles huge data and is slow and tedious; it relies on financial statements that suffer from subjectivity and inadequate disclosure; and it is long-term, so the market may take time to correct a mispriced share.

fields.prompt_md: Give two limitations of technical analysis a student can quote in an essay.
fields.answer_md: It cannot give certain predictions (only 'likely' outcomes), and chart reading is subjective so different analysts read the same chart differently. It also ignores the reasons (fundamentals) behind price moves.

fields.text_md: Fundamental analysis runs top-down through {{c1::economy}}, then {{c2::industry}}, then {{c3::company}}; the bottom-up approach starts directly with the {{c4::company}}.
The five life cycle stages: {{c1::pioneering}}, {{c2::rapid accelerating growth}}, {{c3::mature growth}}, {{c4::stabilisation}}, {{c5::decline}}.
Porter's forces: {{c1::new entrants}}, {{c2::rivalry}}, {{c3::substitutes}}, {{c4::buyers}} (and suppliers).
Sustainable growth = {{c1::retention ratio}} x {{c2::ROE}}; retention ratio = 1 - {{c3::payout ratio}}.
DuPont: ROE = net margin x {{c1::asset turnover}} x {{c2::equity multiplier}}.
Market price (growing dividend) = {{c1::D1}} / ({{c2::Ke - g}}); constant dividend: D / {{c3::Ke}}; EPS method: EPS / {{c4::Ke}}.
Order of preference for market value methods: {{c1::growth-based}}, then {{c2::EPS-based}}, then {{c3::constant dividend}}.
In SWOT, {{c1::strengths}} and {{c2::weaknesses}} are internal factors while {{c3::opportunities}} and {{c4::threats}} are external factors.
RSI = 100 - 100/(1 + RS), where RS = {{c1::average gain}} / {{c2::average loss}}.
Stochastic %K = (close - {{c1::lowest low}}) / ({{c2::highest high}} - lowest low) x 100.
A white candlestick body means close is {{c1::above}} the open (bullish); a black body means close is {{c2::below}} the open (bearish).
Head and shoulders: price cutting the neckline from {{c1::above}} signals a bear market; the inverted pattern piercing the neckline from {{c2::below}} signals a bull market.
Technical analysis views: {{c1::price}}, {{c2::time}}, {{c3::volume}} and {{c4::width}}.
Elliott: waves {{c1::1, 3 and 5}} are impulsive; waves {{c2::2 and 4}} are corrective.
Technical analysis premises: price {{c1::discounts everything}}; prices {{c2::trend}}; {{c3::what}} matters more than why.
